intro: Last month the argument about AI in schools was mostly opinion. This month it has numbers, dates, and contracts attached. New York City shut off generative AI for about 600,000 students through 8th grade, Los Angeles followed within hours, and the teachers unions got Microsoft to sign a student data privacy standard that takes effect November 1. The OECD's PISA results landed the same week, with a 28 point science gap between students who never use AI and those who use it daily, and the head of PISA wrote it up in The Economist under a headline that does not hedge. The Gemini in Classroom change we flagged in September is now getting the national coverage it deserved, and it is still the one setting worth confirming on our own system.

editor_pick.title: Teachers unions announce AI safety agreement with Microsoft
editor_pick.blurb: This is the rare policy story with a date and an action attached. The AFT negotiated a legally enforceable standard with Microsoft: no training AI models on student or educator data, no selling it, no advertising use, and the district keeps control over retention and deletion. It takes effect November 1, it is open to every district in the country, and it can be added to a new or existing Microsoft contract without renegotiating anything. We run on Microsoft. That makes this a question to ask, not a project to start.

sections.name: Leading & Policy
sections.sub: For the people making the calls

items.title: Nation's largest school district bans AI in the classroom through 8th grade
items.takeaway: A one year moratorium on generative AI for roughly 600,000 New York City students, pre-K through 8th grade, and they are disabling the AI components of more than 38 programs that were previously allowed. High school keeps a limited slate of tools plus an AI critical thinking course. The line worth noticing is the teacher carve out: staff can still use AI for lesson planning and operational work, but not for grading or assessment.

items.title: Parents worry about ed tech. Most still see a place for it, polls suggest.
items.takeaway: Useful counterweight if you are hearing that parents want screens gone. Of the parents who support screen time limits, just 1 percent said zero screen time in school. More than 80 percent support laptops. And 53 percent said learning to use AI tools matters for their kid's career. The complaint is about dosage, not about devices.

items.title: Microsoft commits to sweeping AI privacy rules for students. Will other tech giants follow?
items.takeaway: Same agreement as the pick up top, different question: who else signs? OpenAI and Anthropic say they are in talks with the AFT on similar terms. Google has not said either way, which matters because Classroom reaches 150 million teachers and students. Read it for the question to ask the next vendor who comes through the door: will you put this in writing?

items.title: AI backlash comes to the classroom
items.takeaway: The best single screen summary of the moment, and the only place you will find the teacher survey numbers. From an NPR and Ipsos poll: 55 percent of teachers say students mostly use AI to avoid work, 57 percent say it is harder to tell what students actually know, and more than half say their school has given them no guidance at all. That last one is the only number on this page we can do something about.

items.title: This university built an AI curriculum before ChatGPT. Now it wants to help other schools do the same
items.takeaway: The counterweight to the ban stories. Florida started embedding AI across every major in 2022, before ChatGPT was public, on a $95 million build with 100 new faculty and 200 plus courses. The number to carry into a CTE or advising conversation: more than a third of entry level job listings required AI skills in spring 2026, nearly triple the fall 2025 figure.

items.title: Building an everyday equitable practice for AI in schools
items.takeaway: A commentary piece, but it names the gap nobody wants to fund: low poverty districts are nearly twice as likely to give teachers formal AI training as underfunded ones. Training is the equity lever here, not device counts. It also points to Minnesota's Guiding Principles for AI in Education as a framework worth borrowing rather than writing from scratch.

items.title: This Unbelievable AI Minor Program Is Quietly Reshaping Every Student's Future
items.takeaway: Ignore the headline, which is doing a lot of work. The useful part is the shape of what colleges are now building: a 15 to 18 hour AI minor that is less about coding and more about AI literacy, ethics, bias, and judging output. That is a preview of what our graduates will walk into, and it is a commentary blog rather than reported news, so read it as a sketch.

items.title: Stop Counting Screen Minutes. Let's Study Whether Technology Helps Or Hurts Instead
items.takeaway: A short argument for retiring screen time as the metric. Counting minutes tells you nothing about whether the technology helped a student learn, and Boser makes the case for studying the effect instead of the exposure. Pairs well with the Chalkbeat polling above, where it turned out parents were arguing about what the screen is for, not how long it is on.

items.title: How to Cocreate AI Agreements With Students
items.takeaway: The most usable thing in this issue for a classroom teacher. Instead of handing down rules, three named teachers built them with students: a Chicago ELA teacher who worked with her class to keep AI out of brainstorming, personal narratives, and reflection, and a San Diego psych teacher who asked Canva for a picture of a lawyer, got only older white men, and turned it into the bias lesson. Rules students helped write are rules students can explain.

items.title: Parents Are Bringing AI to the IEP Meeting. How Should Teachers Respond?
items.takeaway: This is already happening and most teams have no script for it. Parents are using AI to translate the jargon, check their rights, and draft home goals, which is genuinely good. The head of the special education administrators group also warns that AI assisted parent input can arrive at 20 or 30 pages. The suggested move is transparency both directions, not a policy change.

items.title: How AI Taught Me to Embrace Vulnerability in the Classroom
items.takeaway: A Title I high school teacher working with English learners writes about trying things before she felt ready. Her line is the one to pass along to anyone who thinks they are behind: she stopped believing she had to master AI before she could use it well. She also names the real barriers in her building, which are broken laptops and slow internet, not philosophy.

items.title: When my school banned cell phones, here's what we got back
items.takeaway: An Indianapolis science teacher on year two of a statewide phone ban, which is roughly the phase Tennessee is entering. He teaches the same self control lesson he taught to a silent room in 2021 and now gets a class that participates. He also concedes up front that the research shows bans do not move test scores or attendance, and argues that was never the point. Opinion, and an honest one.

items.title: Students not yet dissuaded by AI exposure in choice of degree subject, report says
items.takeaway: One for anyone advising students on pathways. A King's College London study tracked 1,090 degree programs from 2020 to 2025 against millions of LinkedIn profiles. After ChatGPT launched, the more exposed a degree was to AI, the more its applications grew, about 6 percent for each step up in exposure, while entry level openings in those same fields fell. UK data, so treat it as an early signal rather than a forecast, but computing and engineering are the fields in question.

items.title: What's New in Microsoft EDU, Back to School August 2026
items.takeaway: The most useful item here for us, because it is already paid for. Microsoft Learning Zone now builds interactive lessons of up to 10 slides on any Windows 11 PC instead of requiring a Copilot+ machine (through August 2027), which moves it from someday to now. It also added live teacher-led sessions where students join from their own devices and you watch understanding data come in. Unit Plans, the most requested Teach tool, was slated for September. Included with Microsoft Education licenses at no extra cost.

items.title: Print It, Project It, or Skip the Screen: How Brisk Fits Any Classroom
items.takeaway: Worth a look if you are cutting screen time but still want the prep help. Brisk's new printables generator turns a digital resource into pen and paper work: Frayer models, KWL charts, Venn diagrams, worksheets. It also reads Google Sheets and Excel now, so you can point it at a spreadsheet and get an activity out of it, and it will generate several reading levels of the same resource in one pass. Free Chrome extension, so you can test it this week without a purchase order.

items.title: Claude for Teachers adds lesson prep and math checks built with Learning Commons
items.takeaway: Two new teaching skills: one that walks you through an upcoming lesson and flags where students are likely to get stuck, and one that generates short one to three item math checks tied to a specific standard. Claude for Teachers is moving to a free district level offering rather than individual accounts. This is trade coverage of a vendor announcement, so there is no independent efficacy data yet, but the price is right.

items.title: Notebooks in Gemini, now for schools and organizations
items.takeaway: Source grounded AI, meaning it answers only from documents you upload, is now inside the Gemini app rather than a separate product. Upload your standards, a rubric, and a lesson template, then generate aligned materials and feedback that stay tied to those files. Up to 10 sources per notebook. Rollout started September 14. Note it is admin gated, so both Gemini and Gemini Notebook have to be enabled for you to see it.

items.title: Start the year AI-ready with the Google AI Educator Series
items.takeaway: Free modules under 15 minutes each, one badge apiece, with new topics dropping the first Wednesday of every month. That is about the only PD format that survives a real teacher's week, and the monthly cadence makes it an easy standing item for a faculty meeting. ISTE and ASCD run free companion webinars on Fridays if you want the live version.

items.title: Day of AI launches a free, grade-by-grade PreK-12 AI literacy curriculum
items.takeaway: A full PreK-12 scope and sequence for AI literacy, free, from a nonprofit that came out of MIT. Three grade bands with lesson plans, slide decks, student activities, assessments, and PD. The part that makes it easier to hand to teachers than anything from an AI company: it is tool agnostic and does not push a product.

sections.name: Proceed With Caution
sections.note: Not reasons to avoid AI. Reasons to go in with your eyes open.

items.title: Stop turning schoolchildren into crash-test dummies
items.takeaway: The head of PISA, writing the week the 2025 results came out, and the argument is in the title. Across 760,000 fifteen year olds in 91 countries, students who never use AI for schoolwork scored 509 in science. Daily users scored 481. That 28 point gap is about a year and a half of teaching. The exception is the part worth reading twice: students who used AI weekly, and specifically to help them learn, beat everyone, including the non users. His line is that learning is a productive struggle with new material, and AI either scaffolds that struggle or short circuits it. Paywalled, but the OECD's own summary of the findings is free.

items.title: Schools Caught Flat-Footed After Google Makes Gemini Chatbot Available to All Students
items.takeaway: We flagged this in September and it is still worth confirming. In August, Google opened the Gemini tab in Classroom to K-12 students of all ages instead of 18 and up. The catch that matters: it only appears where a district had already granted students access to Gemini, so if it was off for students it stays off. Compare defaults before you panic. Microsoft Copilot ships off for student accounts, OpenAI's free teacher workspace excludes students, and Anthropic bars minors outright. As one expert puts it, Google defaults to adoption rather than permission.

items.title: What is AI's role in the special education dispute resolution process?
items.takeaway: The place where AI misuse stops being a reputation problem and becomes a legal one. State dispute agencies report complaints running hundreds of pages with AI hallucinated case law in them. On our side of the table, 57 percent of school staff used AI to help write IEPs and 504 plans in 2025, up 18 points in a year. Written state complaints rose 56 percent across 35 states over two years, and nobody is claiming AI caused that, but an IEP that reads generic is the document a hearing officer reads closely.

items.title: Schools Spend Billions on AI, But Struggle to Figure Out What's Worth Buying
items.takeaway: Read this one before the next renewal. The number that should stop you: districts have access to an average of 3,001 digital tools and educators actually use an average of 4. LA Unified paid $3 million for an AI chatbot from a vendor that then filed for bankruptcy. A Tennessee district appears in it too, so this is not a coastal story. The risk is not one bad AI contract, it is a stack of licenses nobody opens.

items.title: Voters express broad concerns about AI and tech in schools, survey shows
items.takeaway: Worth knowing before any AI rollout gets announced publicly. In a Century Foundation survey of more than 2,000 voters, 85 percent worry about students using AI to finish work without learning, 81 percent worry teachers are being pressured into tools with no proven benefit, and 77 percent want guardrails on school technology, including 80 percent of Republicans and 76 percent of Democrats. Note the poll was fielded in May. The takeaway is that skepticism here is bipartisan, which makes it a shared starting point rather than a fight.

items.title: AI Videos Are Warping Early Learning, Teachers Say
items.takeaway: For our pre-K and primary teachers, and honestly for parents. One YouTube channel has put out nearly 5,500 AI generated videos in under a year. The problem is not that they look bad, it is that they look educational and are not, and small children absorb the errors. The American Academy of Pediatrics has a Stop, Wait, Go framework for screening kids' content, and one New York preschool sends families a weekly list of vetted resources, which is a copyable move.

items.title: The "Nonexistent" Research on AI's Benefits for Education
items.takeaway: Higher ed focused, but the argument applies to anything we buy. MIT's Justin Reich says the evidence base for AI in education is almost nonexistent, because rigorous testing takes years and the models now change every one to three months. One researcher found peer reviewed studies claiming AI effectiveness that rest on misapplied or miscalculated statistics. That churn is also why a pilot's results may not survive to the renewal.

items.title: The Big Flaw With Ed-Tech Tutoring Isn't Technological
items.takeaway: Rick Hess and Michael Horn on what they call the 5 percent problem: only a small share of students ever use an AI tutoring tool the way it was designed to be used. The tool works, the usage does not happen, and the license renews anyway. Horn's fix is a schedule change rather than a purchase, which is protected blocks of time so every student actually hits minimum usage. Opinion, and EdWeek meters after a few reads.

items.title: Edtech leader Keith Krueger warns of new threat to E-rate
items.takeaway: The only item in this issue with a live deadline. CoSN's Keith Krueger calls a proposed federal rulemaking an existential threat to E-rate, a 30 year old program worth roughly $3 billion a year, and comments are due October 13. His argument is the one a district would actually submit: E-rate funded networks no longer just carry classroom internet, they carry the student information system, payroll, and the door locks. There is a lookup tool at saveourerate.com.

items.title: Khan Academy's founder on AI: Hope isn't a strategy
items.takeaway: Sal Khan making the case that districts need an actual plan instead of waiting to see how this shakes out. He predicts pockets of pain in the job market within five years rather than an apocalypse, and argues the durable skills are the part school still owns. If your building uses Khan Academy, the Khanmigo updates near the end are the practical part.

items.title: Episode 282: What happens when districts adopt agentic AI?
items.takeaway: The operations conversation most AI education podcasts skip. Agentic AI means AI that acts on your systems instead of just answering questions, and they walk through what that looks like on rostering, procurement, device management, and cameras. If you sit on the technology, HR, or purchasing side, this is the one for you.

challenge.title: Could a student in your room explain your AI rule?
challenge.body: The Edutopia piece in the classroom section has teachers writing AI rules with students instead of for them. So here is the test. If I walked into your classroom and asked a student what they are allowed to use AI for, what would they say? Tell me what your rule actually is, and whether it would survive that question. No names, no judgment. I am collecting these to see how far apart we are.

deck.label: Analog Inspiration
deck.title: Two cards to try this month
deck.note: Two more from the Analog Inspiration deck I picked up at ETSU's Conference for High-Impact Instructional Practices. One teacher move, one student move, every month. Both of these are about slowing down just long enough for the thinking to happen.

cards.name: Critique
cards.image_alt: Analog Inspiration card titled Critique, instructing teachers to prompt AI for a passable but uninspired response to one of their assignments, share it with students along with the rubric, have students evaluate it individually and then with a partner, and close with a class debrief on assignment criteria
cards.headline: Let AI do your assignment badly, then let students grade it.
cards.body: Ask AI for a response to one of your assignments that would pass but not impress. Hand that out with your rubric. Students score it on their own first, then pair up to compare and calibrate, then you debrief as a class. By the end they have argued their way to a shared understanding of what good actually looks like on this assignment, which is a conversation that usually never happens.
cards.try: Students are harder graders than we are. That is the whole trick.

cards.name: Discernment
cards.image_alt: Analog Inspiration card titled Discernment, prompting students to pause and ask what am I trying to avoid by using AI right now, consider whether it is confusion, perfectionism, or boredom, and jot down the observation before continuing
cards.headline: Before you use AI, ask what you are avoiding.
cards.body: The question is one line: what am I trying to avoid by using AI right now? Confusion? Perfectionism? Boredom? Sometimes the honest answer is that the work is hard, and hard is where the learning was going to happen. Have students jot down what they notice. A thirty second pause is enough to turn reaching for AI into a decision instead of a reflex.
cards.try: This one works on adults. I tried it on myself and did not love the answer.
